title: Miss Universe is embroiled in chaos. Again | CNN
text:
Miss Universe’s 75th edition in Puerto Rico is still a day away, but this year’s controversies already include — but are, by no means, limited to — franchise disputes, a protest withdrawal, absent pageant co-owners, visa rejections and a shoddy unofficial runway event that saw contestants struggle to navigate a sandy beach in high heels. And there’s still Tuesday’s grand finale to come.

The contestant list tells some of the story. Half of Southeast Asia is unrepresented this year due to a contractual dispute between organizers and businessman Nawat Itsaragrisil, who runs qualifying pageants in Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Singapore, Vietnam and his native Thailand. (It was, incidentally, Itsaragrisil who sparked last year’s walkout by criticizing eventual winner, Miss Mexico Fátima Bosch, in front of other contestants. He later apologized but denied calling her “dumb head.”)

The disagreement appears to be exacerbated by the Miss Universe Organization’s messy ownership structure, which divides control between the seemingly-at-war MU East and MU West (more on that later), and a decentralized qualifying structure that licenses out national pageants to a who’s-who of local businesspeople in over 100 countries.

Elsewhere, participants from Nepal and five African countries, including would-be debutants South Sudan and the Republic of Congo, have been forced to pull out due to US visa issues. The organizers of the Miss France pageant, meanwhile,withdrewtheir delegate in May in protest against last year’s turmoil — much of which centered on former judge Omar Harfouch’s claim that Bosch’s victory was pre-scripted, and that finalists were preselected in a “secret vote” by an unofficial “impromptu jury.”

Miss Universe Organization has consistently denied the allegations. It also proceeded toform a selection committeethat appointed a new Miss France, whohastraveled to Puerto Rico for the final.

What organizershaven’tdone over the last year is rebuild confidence in the judging process.

The criteria on which the women are ranked have always been broad and subjective, with no meaningful information ever published on how scores are assigned or weighted. Independent auditors like Ernst & Young, which once oversaw voting and handed hosts the results in sealed envelopes on stage, are now nowhere to be seen. Doubts about this year’s process have been compounded by organizers’ failure to reveal, at the time of publication, the identity ofanyjudges for this year’s finale. By contrast, some of last year’s jury, including Harfouch, were announced weeks or even months in advance.

“I would like contestants to know who will judge them, how the judges are selected, how scores are verified, and how conflicts of interest are handled,” Itsaragrisil told CNN via text message, adding that he hopes his six withdrawn Southeast Asian delegates can instead participate next year.

Even die-hard fans are questioning Miss Universe’s future. Comments to avideoposted on social mediaby pageant analyst Luis Portelles,who urged the organization to reveal this year’s judging panel ahead of the closed-door interview portion (“just tell us… release it!”) ranged from renewed allegations of a “cooked”result to calls for a boycott. As one fed-up commenter wrote, “Does it matter anymore?”

In another hangover from last year’s tumult, former Miss Jamaica Gabrielle Henry recently filed a lawsuit against the Miss Universe Organization. In it, she accuses organizers of “negligence” over a head injury she said she sustained after falling off stage during a 2025 preliminary event. Litigation is ongoing, and the Miss Universe Organization did not respond to CNN’s request for comment on the case.

This may, however, be the least of organizers’ legal troubles. Simmering in the background of this already shambolic event are the scandal-plagued affairs of the pageant’s co-owners.

Last year, Anne Jakrajutatip, founder of MU East’s owner JKN Global Group, was sentenced, in absentia, to two years in prison for fraud involving a 30-million-baht ($885,000) corporate bond investment, according to Thai media. The businesswoman and transgender rights activist failed to appear at a Bangkok court in December and now is considered at large.

The Miss Universe Organization, which Jakrajutatippurchased for $20 millionin 2022,announcedlast October that she had been replaced as CEO. And with JKN Global recently placed into receivership by a Thai bankruptcy court, her company’s part-ownership of Miss Universe has been thrown in doubt anyway. (Itsaragrisil, the Southeast Asian franchisee, claimshenow effectively runs MU East, though his role is disputed by counterparts from the Western bloc.)

On the pageant’s other side is Raúl Rocha Cantú, whose Legacy Holding Group owns MU West. The controversial Mexican businessman was at the center of last year’s tumult, accused by Harfouch of rigging the vote in Bosch’s favor because of apparent business ties to her father, an allegation Rocha Cantú vociferously denied. He then openly admitted on a livestream that the relative weakness of hotly tipped Miss Ivory Coast’s passport had counted against her, as she would need numerous visas to complete her globe-trotting duties as Miss Universe.

In sum, the dumpster fire that is Miss Universe is burning more fiercely than ever. But is anyone even looking? In much of the West, increasingly not.

Once a fixture on primetime network television, the English-language broadcast of the “Super Bowl” of pageants now only appears on streaming platforms in the US. The rapid decline in mainstream American viewership mirrors the fortunes of other pageants. Miss World is now on streaming service Fawesome; Miss USA and Miss America air on the specialist platforms Queen Beauty Network and PageantVision, respectively.

It’s enough to make the era of Donald Trump, who owned Miss Universe from 1996 to the early 2000s, before co-owning it with NBC until 2015, look like veritable golden years. And commercially speaking, they may have been, according to Hilary Levey Friedman, a sociologist and author of thebook“Here She Is: The Complicated Reign of the Beauty Pageant in America.”

“A lot of their problems started after Donald Trump sold Miss Universe and Miss USA,” she said over the phone, adding that controversies over the now-US president’s ownership — including allegations he walked into dressing rooms while women were undressed or getting changed — only emerged after he sold the pageants and ran for office. A spokesperson from Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign denied the claims at the time.

“There used to be, particularly with Miss Universe, way more stability in terms of who the owners were and who was running it,” Friedman said, adding: “There’s just been a lot more turnover in the past few years.”

Pageants’ commercial challenges are symptomatic of wider societal shifts. In the US, like many parts of the world, the events are increasingly seen as anachronisms that objectify women and promote singular beauty standards.

Miss Universe’s recent attempts to modernize have done little to dispel this notion. The pageant’s decision to allow — gasp — mothers and married women to participate, starting in 2023, only served to remind everyone that, in this decade, mothers and married womenhadn’tbeen able to take part. A rule banning over-28s was only lifted in 2024.

Other rule changes have, arguably, helped dismantle prejudices. For one, Miss Universe has allowed trans women to participate since 2013 (although only after beauty queen Jenna Talackova wascontroversially disqualifiedfrom Miss Universe Canada). Progress on who canenteris not the same as whowins, however.

“The same body types tend to win — we’ve seen an expansion of racial and ethnic diversity, sexuality, even some gender identity, but not so much different body types,” said Friedman, describing the “very real psychological issues” contestants may face due as a result.

“Whenever you’re in a competition, you’re going to think, ‘Well, I just wasn’t good enough,’” she said. “And when this has to do with how you look, people will think, ‘Oh, I’m not thin enough, I’m not tall enough, I’m not ‘whatever’ enough.’ And that can be very difficult, because some of those are just immutable things about ourselves.”

Miss Universe also perseveres with its hopelessly outdated swimsuit contest, launched in the early 1950s — an era it feels better suited to — as a marketing stunt for a swimwear manufacturer. More than seven decades on, the competition is still essentially a judged bikini parade (aside from a handful of contestants permitted to wear more modest burkinis on religious grounds.)

While hardly constituting radical enlightenment, pageants like Miss World and Miss America have at least replaced their swimwear rounds with alternatives, including “athleisure.” Even then, however, the focus is often how your body looks not “what your body does,” Friedman said.

But pageants’ ability to impact wider beauty standards is likely tempered by their declining social relevance, the author added. After all, compared to the events’ 1950s and ‘60s heyday, women and girls now contend with myriad other sources of unrealistic body ideals, whether reality TV or social media.

It is possible to question the role of pageants in modern society while also enjoying the spectacle they bring. Take Miss Universe’s unashamedly bonkers national costume parade, which on Saturday saw contestants dress up in patriotic costumes resembling anything from a troll (Norway) to a golden frog (Costa Rica). Even then, though, the pageants couldn’t dodge controversy entirely, with Miss Israel audibly booed by audience members after unveiling the word “peace,” in three different languages, on her costume’s cape.

On Tuesday, viewing parties will be held around the world, including in the parts of Africa, Asia and Latin America where pageantry enjoys continued, even growing, popularity. The show will be a source of pride for those who enjoy seeing — and cheering on — their country on the world stage. Think, especially, of pageant fans in Saint Martin and Uganda, which are making their Miss Universe debuts this year, or in Jordan and Tunisia, which are competing for the first time since 1960 and 1971, respectively.

In many countries, pageants are everyday community events, while winning national competitions can present life-changing opportunities to young women. Even in the US, pageantry’s reputation differs by culture: Despite Miss Universe’s declining fortunes on American TV, the Spanish-language broadcast of 2025’s finale was viewed by2.6 million peopleon Telemundo, up from 2.1 million the previous year.

And while the chaos surrounding this year’s Miss Universe may make for car-crash viewing, there’s a human cost too.

Take Miss Singapore, Vion Tan, whowroteon Instagram that her forced withdrawal had “hit me harder than I can put into words.”

“This journey was never just about a crown or a competition,” she added. “It was about the opportunity to carry Singapore’s name onto an international stage, to share our culture, our stories and the spirit of a small nation with big dreams.”
